passages.title: Vashti refuses the king
passages.summary: King Ahasuerus rules one hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia. In his third year he displays his wealth for six months. He then gives a seven-day feast in the palace garden. Queen Vashti holds a feast for the women. On the seventh day the king, merry with wine, sends for her. She refuses to come. His advisers fear that all wives will now despise their husbands. A royal law removes Vashti and orders every man to rule his house.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson starts with the decision to replace Vashti. How do the advisers turn one refusal into rules for wives?

contextNote.title: A court turns one refusal into a household rule
contextNote.text: The text gives no reason for Vashti’s refusal. The king can command a hundred twenty-seven provinces and not his wife. He asks his advisers what the law allows (verse 15). Memucan turns one refusal into a danger to every household (verses 17–18). Verse 20 expects a decree to produce honor for all husbands. The law is written so that it cannot be changed (verse 19). That kind of law will matter again in chapters 3 and 8.

passages.title: Esther becomes queen
passages.summary: The king’s servants propose gathering beautiful young women for him to choose from. Mordecai, a Jew of Benjamin, lives in Susa. He has raised his orphaned cousin Esther as a daughter. Esther is taken to the palace and wins the keeper’s favor. She does not reveal her people, as Mordecai told her. After a year of preparation she goes to the king. He loves her more than the others and makes her queen. Mordecai uncovers a plot to kill the king, and it is written in the records.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Esther names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Mordecai’s care for Esther. How does he help her after she becomes queen?

contextNote.title: Access to the court does not equal freedom
contextNote.text: Esther gains favor while keeping her family identity concealed. Verses 8 and 16 say she “was taken.” Verse 12 requires a year of oils and perfumes. The Egyptian perfume vessel shown is far older and only a comparison. Verse 20 shows her still obeying Mordecai as queen. Mordecai’s report in verses 21–23 is recorded and not rewarded. That second hidden fact will later change the court.

passages.title: Haman orders the Jews’ deaths
passages.summary: The king promotes Haman the Agagite above all the officials. Everyone at the gate bows to him except Mordecai. Haman learns Mordecai is a Jew and decides to destroy all Jews. He casts lots to choose a day. He tells the king that a certain people ignores the king’s laws. He offers a huge sum, and the king gives him his ring. Letters go to every province to kill all Jews on one day. The king and Haman sit down to drink, and Susa is confused.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Haman’s anger. How does his anger at Mordecai threaten all the Jews?

contextNote.title: A written order carries danger across distance
contextNote.text: Haman never names the people, and the king never asks (verse 8). Verse 12 then shows the machinery of rule at work. Scribes write in every script and language, and the ring seals it. A bulla shows the kind of impression a seal left on clay. Couriers carry the order to each province (verse 13). A court decision can reach households far from the palace. Haman is an Agagite, and Mordecai descends from Kish (2:5; 1 Samuel 15:8).

passages.title: Esther decides to approach the king
passages.summary: Mordecai tears his clothes and wails in sackcloth at the king’s gate. Jews in every province fast and weep. Esther sends a servant to learn what has happened. Mordecai sends a copy of the decree and asks her to plead with the king. She answers that anyone who approaches unsummoned may die. Mordecai replies that she will not escape in the palace. Esther asks all the Jews of Susa to fast three days. She will go to the king: “If I perish, I perish.”
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies courage and fasting. What help does Esther ask for before approaching the king?

contextNote.title: The palace cannot separate one person from a threatened people
contextNote.text: The book of Esther never names God. Verse 14 comes closest with “another place.” Mordecai’s argument has two parts. The palace will not protect her, and help will come somehow. His question, “Who knows,” claims no certainty about her purpose. Until now Esther has obeyed Mordecai (2:20). In verses 16–17 she gives the orders, and he carries them out.

passages.title: Two invitations and Haman’s anger
passages.summary: On the third day Esther puts on royal robes and stands in the inner court. The king holds out his golden scepter and offers her up to half the kingdom. She invites him and Haman to a banquet. At the banquet she invites them to a second one tomorrow. Haman leaves happy until he sees Mordecai, who will not rise. At home he boasts of his riches, sons, and honors. He says none of it satisfies him while Mordecai sits at the gate. His wife suggests a gallows fifty cubits high.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me compares Esther’s risk with Haman’s pride. Why do his honors fail to satisfy him?

contextNote.title: Honor does not satisfy a demand for submission
contextNote.text: Haman lists his honors in verses 11–12. He has wealth, many sons, rank, and the queen’s private invitation. Verse 13 cancels all of it with one man at the gate. His joy depends on every person’s submission. One refusal is therefore enough to spoil it. His wife and friends offer a remedy: kill the man (verse 14). The text does not explain why Esther delays her request twice.

passages.title: Haman must honor Mordecai
passages.summary: That night the king cannot sleep and has the royal records read to him. He hears how Mordecai exposed the plot against him. He learns that Mordecai received nothing. Haman arrives to ask for Mordecai’s death. The king asks how to honor a man the king favors. Haman thinks this means himself and describes a royal robe and horse. The king tells him to do all this for Mordecai. Haman leads Mordecai through the city and goes home in mourning.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: The Seminary lesson recalls the king’s records. How does the saved report change Mordecai’s treatment?

contextNote.title: An unread reward becomes the turning point
contextNote.text: Verse 1 begins with a small thing: the king could not sleep. The reading happens to reach Mordecai’s report (verse 2). Haman happens to arrive at that moment (verse 4). The text names no cause for any of this. It says only “On that night.” Many readers see God’s hand in such timing, though the book never says so. A good deed left unrewarded in 2:23 becomes the turning point.

passages.title: Esther names Haman as the enemy
passages.summary: The king and Haman come to Esther’s second banquet. The king again asks what she wants. She asks for her life and the life of her people. They have been sold to be destroyed. The king asks who has dared to do this. Esther answers, “An adversary and an enemy, even this wicked Haman!” The king storms out and returns to find Haman fallen on Esther’s couch. Haman is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Haman’s choices and their results. How does Esther explain the danger to the king?

contextNote.title: Esther gives the policy a face the king recognizes
contextNote.text: Esther’s first words join her life to her people’s (verse 3). She has hidden that tie since 2:10. In verse 4 she uses the decree’s own three verbs for killing (3:13). She says “sold,” which recalls Haman’s silver (3:9). The king approved the order without asking who would die. Now the policy has a face he knows. She adds that she would have kept silent about slavery alone.

passages.title: New orders allow the Jews to fight
passages.summary: The king gives Haman’s estate to Esther and his ring to Mordecai. Esther falls at the king’s feet and weeps. She begs him to cancel Haman’s letters. The king says a sealed decree cannot be reversed. He lets them write a new one in his name. It allows the Jews in every city to gather and defend their lives. Couriers ride out on royal horses. Mordecai leaves in royal robes, and Susa rejoices.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies fasting during danger. Why must Esther keep asking for help after Haman dies?

contextNote.title: A new letter must answer an existing order
contextNote.text: Haman is dead, and his decree still stands. Esther’s plea in verses 3–6 shows that killing him removed nothing. Verse 8 says a sealed decree cannot be cancelled, only answered. A bulla shows the kind of impression a seal left on clay. So her success needs further writing, messengers, and permission to gather. The second letter mirrors the first almost phrase by phrase (verse 11; 3:13). The threatened people need protection that reaches beyond the palace.

passages.title: Victory, violence, and Purim
passages.summary: On the thirteenth day of Adar the Jews gather and strike those who attack them. Officials help them out of fear of Mordecai. In Susa they kill five hundred men and Haman’s ten sons. Esther asks for a second day in Susa. Across the provinces seventy-five thousand enemies die. The Jews take no plunder. They rest and feast on the next day. Mordecai and Esther write letters that make the feast of Purim yearly.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Esther’s courage with later joy. How do gifts help people remember the rescue?

contextNote.title: A festival keeps both grief and survival in memory
contextNote.text: Verse 22 defines the feast by a reversal. Sorrow became gladness, and mourning became a holiday. The verse also says how to keep it. People send food to one another and gifts to the poor. Verses 10, 15, and 16 repeat that no plunder was taken. The decree had allowed it (8:11). The text states the number of dead plainly and without comment.

passages.title: Mordecai serves his people
passages.summary: King Ahasuerus lays a tax on the land and the coasts. His acts of power are written in the royal records. The records also tell of the greatness of Mordecai. Mordecai the Jew is second to the king. He is great among the Jews and well liked by his many kin. He seeks the good of his people. He speaks peace to all their children.
passages.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Mordecai works for his people’s good. Who benefits from the power he receives?

contextNote.title: High office receives a measure beyond personal honor
contextNote.text: The last chapter is three verses long. Verse 1 reports a tax, so the empire goes on as before. The Jews remain subjects of a foreign king. The book does not end with a return to Judah. Verse 3 measures Mordecai’s greatness by two things. He sought his people’s good, and he spoke peace. High office is judged here by whom it serves.

events.detail: Esther’s first words join her life to her people’s (verse 3). She has hidden that tie since 2:10. In verse 4 she uses the decree’s own three verbs for killing (3:13). She says “sold,” which recalls Haman’s silver (3:9). The king approved the order without asking who would die. Now the policy has a face he knows. She adds that she would have kept silent about slavery alone.
events.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Haman’s choices and their results. How does Esther explain the danger to the king?

events.title: New orders allow the Jews to fight
events.summary: The king gives Haman’s estate to Esther and his ring to Mordecai. Esther falls at the king’s feet and weeps. She begs him to cancel Haman’s letters. The king says a sealed decree cannot be reversed. He lets them write a new one in his name. It allows the Jews in every city to gather and defend their lives. Couriers ride out on royal horses. Mordecai leaves in royal robes, and Susa rejoices.
events.detail: Haman is dead, and his decree still stands. Esther’s plea in verses 3–6 shows that killing him removed nothing. Verse 8 says a sealed decree cannot be cancelled, only answered. A bulla shows the kind of impression a seal left on clay. So her success needs further writing, messengers, and permission to gather. The second letter mirrors the first almost phrase by phrase (verse 11; 3:13). The threatened people need protection that reaches beyond the palace.
events.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies fasting during danger. Why must Esther keep asking for help after Haman dies?

events.title: Victory, violence, and Purim
events.summary: On the thirteenth day of Adar the Jews gather and strike those who attack them. Officials help them out of fear of Mordecai. In Susa they kill five hundred men and Haman’s ten sons. Esther asks for a second day in Susa. Across the provinces seventy-five thousand enemies die. The Jews take no plunder. They rest and feast on the next day. Mordecai and Esther write letters that make the feast of Purim yearly.
events.detail: Verse 22 defines the feast by a reversal. Sorrow became gladness, and mourning became a holiday. The verse also says how to keep it. People send food to one another and gifts to the poor. Verses 10, 15, and 16 repeat that no plunder was taken. The decree had allowed it (8:11). The text states the number of dead plainly and without comment.
events.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Esther’s courage with later joy. How do gifts help people remember the rescue?

events.title: Mordecai serves his people
events.summary: King Ahasuerus lays a tax on the land and the coasts. His acts of power are written in the royal records. The records also tell of the greatness of Mordecai. Mordecai the Jew is second to the king. He is great among the Jews and well liked by his many kin. He seeks the good of his people. He speaks peace to all their children.
events.detail: The last chapter is three verses long. Verse 1 reports a tax, so the empire goes on as before. The Jews remain subjects of a foreign king. The book does not end with a return to Judah. Verse 3 measures Mordecai’s greatness by two things. He sought his people’s good, and he spoke peace. High office is judged here by whom it serves.
events.uncertainty: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

lds.text: Mordecai works for his people’s good. Who benefits from the power he receives?

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Persian royal road
ancientRoads.summary: Persian kings kept a road with rest stations from Sardis to Susa. Herodotus counted 111 stations on it.
ancientRoads.detail: Royal messengers changed horses at the stations. Esther 8:10 sends the king’s letters by riders on royal horses.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Herodotus names lands and rivers, not towns. The line between Sardis and Susa is a broad guide.

regions.name: Persian Empire · part shown
regions.summary: Cyrus founded the Persian Empire in 550 BCE and took Babylon in 539 BCE. It reached from Egypt and Asia Minor to the Indus Valley.
regions.detail: Esther opens with a king who rules 127 provinces from Susa. His sealed letters reach every province.
regions.uncertainty: The shape shows only the western part of the empire. Its eastern lands lie off this map.

guides.title: Esther: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: A written order carries danger across distance
steps.text: Haman never names the people, and the king never asks (verse 8). Verse 12 then shows the machinery of rule at work. Scribes write in every script and language, and the ring seals it. A bulla shows the kind of impression a seal left on clay. Couriers carry the order to each province (verse 13). A court decision can reach households far from the palace. Haman is an Agagite, and Mordecai descends from Kish (2:5; 1 Samuel 15:8).

steps.title: An unread reward becomes the turning point
steps.text: Verse 1 begins with a small thing: the king could not sleep. The reading happens to reach Mordecai’s report (verse 2). Haman happens to arrive at that moment (verse 4). The text names no cause for any of this. It says only “On that night.” Many readers see God’s hand in such timing, though the book never says so. A good deed left unrewarded in 2:23 becomes the turning point.

steps.title: A festival keeps both grief and survival in memory
steps.text: Verse 22 defines the feast by a reversal. Sorrow became gladness, and mourning became a holiday. The verse also says how to keep it. People send food to one another and gifts to the poor. Verses 10, 15, and 16 repeat that no plunder was taken. The decree had allowed it (8:11). The text states the number of dead plainly and without comment.

chapterMaps.note: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.
chapterMaps.narrative: King Ahasuerus rules one hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia. In his third year he displays his wealth for six months. He then gives a seven-day feast in the palace garden. Queen Vashti holds a feast for the women. On the seventh day the king, merry with wine, sends for her. She refuses to come. His advisers fear that all wives will now despise their husbands. A royal law removes Vashti and orders every man to rule his house.
chapterMaps.limits: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

chapterMaps.note: Lines join the places Esther names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.
chapterMaps.narrative: The king’s servants propose gathering beautiful young women for him to choose from. Mordecai, a Jew of Benjamin, lives in Susa. He has raised his orphaned cousin Esther as a daughter. Esther is taken to the palace and wins the keeper’s favor. She does not reveal her people, as Mordecai told her. After a year of preparation she goes to the king. He loves her more than the others and makes her queen. Mordecai uncovers a plot to kill the king, and it is written in the records.

chapterMaps.narrative: The king promotes Haman the Agagite above all the officials. Everyone at the gate bows to him except Mordecai. Haman learns Mordecai is a Jew and decides to destroy all Jews. He casts lots to choose a day. He tells the king that a certain people ignores the king’s laws. He offers a huge sum, and the king gives him his ring. Letters go to every province to kill all Jews on one day. The king and Haman sit down to drink, and Susa is confused.

chapterMaps.narrative: Mordecai tears his clothes and wails in sackcloth at the king’s gate. Jews in every province fast and weep. Esther sends a servant to learn what has happened. Mordecai sends a copy of the decree and asks her to plead with the king. She answers that anyone who approaches unsummoned may die. Mordecai replies that she will not escape in the palace. Esther asks all the Jews of Susa to fast three days. She will go to the king: “If I perish, I perish.”
chapterMaps.limits: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

chapterMaps.note: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.
chapterMaps.narrative: On the third day Esther puts on royal robes and stands in the inner court. The king holds out his golden scepter and offers her up to half the kingdom. She invites him and Haman to a banquet. At the banquet she invites them to a second one tomorrow. Haman leaves happy until he sees Mordecai, who will not rise. At home he boasts of his riches, sons, and honors. He says none of it satisfies him while Mordecai sits at the gate. His wife suggests a gallows fifty cubits high.
chapterMaps.limits: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.

chapterMaps.note: Susa marks the story’s setting. Individual rooms and courier roads are not mapped.
chapterMaps.narrative: That night the king cannot sleep and has the royal records read to him. He hears how Mordecai exposed the plot against him. He learns that Mordecai received nothing. Haman arrives to ask for Mordecai’s death. The king asks how to honor a man the king favors. Haman thinks this means himself and describes a royal robe and horse. The king tells him to do all this for Mordecai. Haman leads Mordecai through the city and goes home in mourning.

chapterMaps.narrative: The king and Haman come to Esther’s second banquet. The king again asks what she wants. She asks for her life and the life of her people. They have been sold to be destroyed. The king asks who has dared to do this. Esther answers, “An adversary and an enemy, even this wicked Haman!” The king storms out and returns to find Haman fallen on Esther’s couch. Haman is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.
